That would use up to 5% of a typical 1TB SSD’s rated endurance each year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs. One user measured about 3GB an hour on the susceptible driver, and another mentioned estimated up to 30GB/hour on the newer 621.24. This follows a similar-looking bug from AMD’s video driver discovered last month.

The bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “new in 621.14,” which came out on Nov. 4, who says it operates by “continuously [rewriting] the binary log file” with “real writes” to the drive. The writes are coming from the NVDisplay.Container.exe process, or the “NVIDIA Display Container LS” service, which logs to the nvlog.nvlgstg file. This background service is necessary for running the Nvidia Control Panel and App. It’s not clear what’s written in the log, and not every system is necessarily impacted.

The “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive. The measurements came from Windows Resource Monitor, Windows performance counters, and CrystalDiskInfo. The Data Units Written counter matched Windows’ reporting. This test showed 515MB of process I/O coming with 270MB of total writes to the C: drive over five minutes. That works out to roughly 3GB per hour, in line with the user’s own estimate.

Worse, “the write volume increases as the file grows.” Stopping the service and deleting the log can temporarily reduce the writes. With the previous driver version 621.01, the writes totaled less than 2MB per five minutes, and a second user in the thread confirmed that a rollback helps.

Mitigation attempts, such as three clean reinstalls with the help of DDU from that second user, did not fix the problem. The writing process also impacted gaming and video performance, potentially causing hitching, which suggests it gets worse under load.

Another user, AyzekUorren, in a separate thread about driver 621.24, which came out Nov. 12, says that it could get up to “about 30gb per 1h” or even “70gb or even more” with longer sessions. This is even with telemetry disabled in the Nvidia App. Noted is that every Alt+Tab added 500MB to 1GB of writes, at least for this user.

In AMD’s case, it was the External Events Utility, or atieclxx.exe, that exhibited constant writes on an idle PC. In that case, the AMD utility was reportedly copying its own executable every second. To put the impact into context, the AMD bug had rates reported between 0.3 and 5MB/s while total drive writes in the 621.14 test measured around 0.9MB/s.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The Nvidia numbers are somewhat alarming, given that a typical 1TB SSD is rated for 600TB of writes over a standard five-year warranty. Even at 270MB per five minutes, this could be about 28TB per year — for a never-sleeping PC — which is reaching toward 5% of the drive’s rated endurance, although the writes include everything the system is writing and realistic uptime will be less. However, at the higher end — 30GB per hour, at eight hours a day — one could see 15% of drive endurance worn every year for nothing.

This doesn’t make it a drive killer, but given how much users value drive endurance, especially with SSD prices as they are, avoiding unnecessary writes like this is certainly a priority. To see if you’re affected, check Resource Monitor and look for the telltale NVDisplay.Container.exe and the nvlog.nvlgstg file in the list. You can also check the SMART Data Units Written value with CrystalDiskInfo or equivalent, such as your drive’s SSD toolbox.

At this time, no fix or hotfix has been announced, and the best workaround is to do a rollback. A similar issue in the past, fixed with driver update 471.96 back in 2021, was covered by Nvidia’s release notes. As it stands, Nvidia has “N/A” for 621.24’s Open Issues, and the company has not acknowledged the bug. For the AMD bug, the driver wasn't fixed for over three weeks (and came as an optional update).

#10646. Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves to You

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

#10642. You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a new one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

…you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.)

Email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

You can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this new Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when announced in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”

The company said it 'values its interactions with gamers above all else'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD Japan's X account has been met with sharp reproach after claiming the company loves gamers and values its interactions with gamers above all else, with commenters and even a community note expressing dissent at the sentiment, owing to AMD's comments on its "data center-first" ethos and a commitment to AI that has driven the price of consumer PC gaming up to nearly unaffordable levels.

Quoting a Tom's Hardware post on the X social network discussing CEO Dr. Lisa Su meeting gamers and autographing a GPU, the AMD Japan account was quick to seize the moment. "AMD values its interactions with gamers above all else," the post read, but it was met with a stark reminder that gamers don't feel the same way. The post soon received a new community note that pointed out that AMD's own CEO doesn't agree. In fact, Su was quoted as saying that AMD is now "a data center-first company," with the note also pointing to the fact that AMD's data center revenue increased 97% year-over-year, as per its Q3 2026 earnings report. That equates to around $8.5 billion in revenue, while client and gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Gaming alone was down 40%.

At the time, Su said that AMD expected its server revenue to double year over year in 2027, with its data center AI revenue growing at an even faster rate. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth," the CEO said during the company's earnings call.

ゲーマーとの交流を何よりも大切にするAMD。 コミュニティと直接つながり、その声に耳を傾け続ける姿勢こそAMDの強みです。 AMD loves gamers. 🎮November 17, 2026

By comparison, the same call heard Su say that, in 2027, AMD was "planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage." With this all in mind, it's perhaps no surprise that the AMD Japan X account stirred such a strong response from gamers who feel that AMD has left them behind in search of a more lucrative data center market. AMD is certainly not alone in that regard. Nvidia, once the darling of the PC component enthusiast, is now focused on AI data center components instead. The company's high-performance AI chips are so capable that they're export-controlled, something that, among other reasons, will put former CEO Jensen Huang in front of a House Foreign Affairs panel in December.

As for AMD, its ill-timed, misjudged X post ended with "AMD loves gamers." Gamers would appear to disagree.

#10634. Find Orphan Pages by Comparing Your Sitemap with an Internal Crawl

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A page can return 200 OK, exist in an XML sitemap, and still be practically invisible to anyone browsing the site.

You do not need a full commercial crawler to find the obvious cases. A small Node.js script can compare two things:

Anything present in the first set but missing from the second deserves investigation.

You now have URLs that the application publishes through its sitemap but that your HTML crawl could not reach.

The page might be intentionally isolated. It might exist for a campaign. Navigation might depend on JavaScript. Your crawler may have missed authentication or pagination.

Should a normal visitor reasonably be able to discover this page from another page on the site?

Google recommends using standard crawlable elements with resolvable href values for links that should be discoverable. Google's guidance on crawlable links

That is also good web architecture independent of SEO.

Internal links should not exist merely to move ranking signals around.

They should help users move between related tasks.

A technical guide might lead to a product page. A product page might link back to the configuration guide. A category page should make important child resources discoverable without requiring a user to know the exact URL.

This is why on-page SEO and internal linking are closely connected to site architecture. Good internal links clarify relationships for both visitors and crawlers.

At a broader level, crawlability is one part of technical SEO and search visibility. A page that nobody can reliably discover is difficult to evaluate regardless of how strong its content may be.

If an important URL appears disconnected because navigation is created only after client-side JavaScript runs, the script has surfaced a real architectural fact.

You can then decide whether that is acceptable.

If your application genuinely requires rendered-DOM crawling, replace the fetch-and-Cheerio layer with Playwright.

Do not make the simple crawler pretend to be something it is not.

The best output from this tool is not an "SEO score."

It is a concrete question for the development team:

This page exists. The sitemap knows about it. Why can't a normal HTML crawl reach it?

#10631. 22 leadership insights on ensuring accountability without instilling fear

Accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix. The term can come with negative connotations: If something goes wrong, it means whoever is accountable is to blame. Fearing accountability, some team members may hesitate to take roles that require much of it. Even if they step up, fear can keep them from doing their best work or taking needed risks.

We asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear. Below, 22 of them share their best advice on keeping accountability as a necessary and positive role instead of something people dread.

1. TREAT MISSES AS INFORMATION

Be as clear about expectations up front as you are about results afterward. Fear comes from ambiguity: People don’t know what success looks like until they’ve missed it. I set clear owners and outcomes at the start, then treat misses as information. What did we learn, and what do we change? I also name my own misses out loud, before anyone else’s. When the leader models it, accountability stops feeling like judgment and becomes a shared standard the whole team owns. — Megan Noel, Covista

2. MODEL SELF-REFLECTION

Accountability is less likely to create fear when leaders hold themselves accountable to the same standards and deadlines they expect of others, are honest about where they fell short, and share the lessons they learned. The more leaders model that kind of self-reflection, the more comfortable others will feel doing the same—and helping their teammates build that skill. — Grace Keith Rodriguez, Caliber Corporate Advisers

3. FOCUS ON LESSONS LEARNED

Accountability should give people the confidence to take big swings. When it only shows up for the misses and mistakes, you create a culture of fear, which doesn’t inspire creativity or big thinking. Instead, be clear about expectations, set ambitious goals together, and when something falls short, focus on the lesson learned and move on. — Max Friedman, Givebutter

4. LEAD WITH CURIOSITY RATHER THAN BLAME

Accountability without fear begins with clarity—clear expectations and realistic goals—balanced with my personal commitment to being accessible and providing timely feedback. This shared accountability builds trust as the same standards apply at both levels. When challenges arise, I am able to lead with curiosity rather than blame, asking “What happened, and what support do you need?” which creates space for my team to surface issues early and treat setbacks as learning opportunities. Consistency reinforces this sense of safety, so instead of fearing accountability, my team feels supported and invested in our shared success. — Maurice Twomey, Roto

5. ENSURE REAL ALIGNMENT FROM THE START

Many tend to think of accountability as something you create at the end of a process. Someone didn’t do what they were supposed to do. Will you hold them accountable or not? In my experience, however, accountability issues are often alignment issues in disguise. What are we trying to do and why? By when? What are we both assuming? What is really feasible? Good leaders ensure there is real alignment around these questions at the start of a process. They approach accountability not as a punishment question but as a clarity question—and in doing so, they debunk the idea that accountability and fear must come hand-in-hand. — Maril MacDonald, Gagen MacDonald

6. OWN THE OUTDATED DASHBOARD

Accountability isn’t perfection. A team member flagged outdated targets on a dashboard I was presenting. I owned it and thanked them. Small moments like that set the tone for the big ones. When we miss a real target, we own our work and our choices and solve it as a team. Do that consistently, and you build that muscle for the harder moments. — Michele Walsh, UNICEF USA

7. SHIFT THE MINDSET

When leaders shift their mindset from “don’t break this” to “let’s try this,” accountability becomes about outcomes and learning. As leaders, we need to role model what strong accountability looks like and acknowledge fear with grace and empathy. This means we should understand that some good ideas won’t stick, and we should celebrate innovative thinking even when it doesn’t result in a win. When people see their leader take a smart risk, own what follows, and adapt quickly, they do the same. — Jacqui Canney, ServiceNow

8. CUT THE ENDLESS APPROVAL CHAINS

If you want real accountability, let team members own the outcome and cut the endless approval chains. Nobody likes to fail, but you can build a culture of permissible failure and actually walk the talk. When mistakes happen, address them head-on, take the lesson, and move on fast. — Khozema Shipchandler, Twilio

9. ASK WHAT HAPPENED, NOT WHO DID IT

Make the destination crystal clear and the path flexible. Fear shows up when people don’t know what “good” looks like until they miss it. I’d rather over-communicate the outcome, agree on ownership out loud, and let people choose how they get there. When something goes sideways, my first question is “What happened?” not “Who did this?” Accountability is a promise teammates make to each other, not a punishment waiting to happen. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr

10. MAKE ACCOUNTABILITY A WEEKLY RHYTHM

Accountability works when colleagues do the flagging, not the leader. Every week, especially in our executive meetings, we review our trackers top to bottom and call out anything blocked or at risk, in the open, in front of the team. It’s rare that someone gets blindsided in a one-on-one weeks later. Fear creeps in when accountability feels personal or arbitrary. A visible, weekly rhythm makes it structural instead, and that is what keeps people honest without making them defensive. Consistent communication is key. Beyond email and Slack, good ole phone calls and texts are quite effective. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will

11. TEACH CLEAN ESCALATION

For our team, it all starts with providing clear communication so people understand what’s expected and how success will be measured. We approach conversations from a point of kindness and empathy, which includes listening and practicing radical candor so everyone is provided honest, respectful feedback and knows where they stand. Teaching clean escalation and other techniques also plays a role in maximizing accountability while preserving the best possible team dynamics. When people know they can raise issues early and get help addressing them, taking responsibility becomes much easier. — Leerom Segal, Klick Health

12. DON’T LEAVE PEOPLE GUESSING

Clarity, transparency, and continuous communication. That is the foundation—and frankly, it is the ethos on which we built our company. When people know exactly what is expected, where they stand, and that honest feedback flows early and often, there is nothing to fear. Fear creeps in when people are left guessing. The goal is shared accountability. Not imposed from the top down but owned collectively by a team that feels genuinely empowered. When that culture exists, people hold each other to a higher standard because they want to—not because they have to. — Meredith Rosenberg, NU Advisory Partners

13. THE KIND OF FEAR MATTERS

Fear isn’t always bad. Fearing your boss is different from fearing you didn’t do your best work. Top-down fear can produce compliance, but rarely excellence. I want my team accountable to themselves first, because people only do their best work on things they care about. That means clear quarterly and annual goals, professional development funds for growth areas, honest conversations about where they want to go, and a real grasp of why our work matters and why their contribution is key. People who hold themselves to a standard outperform people who only answer to a boss. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards

14. ATTACH A HUMAN OWNER TO AI-RELATED DECISIONS

I would argue that it is the lack of accountability that creates fear. Accountability should remove ambiguity. Each artificial intelligence-related decision should have a human owner. There are clear rules of engagement that establish what is and is not in the bounds of permissibility. And when mistakes are made, they are inspected and not concealed. Fear breeds in darkness: Create light. — Scott Brighton, Bonterra

15. HAVE EMPLOYEES SET THE BAR FOR THEMSELVES

Accountability is a matter of doing what you commit to. Our team members have some flexibility to set expectations regarding the timing and scope of their deliveries. Publicly demonstrating finished products in team or client meetings improves accountability. Fear is effectively removed when trying to clear bars we set for ourselves. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps

16. SHOW VULNERABILITY

Model that it’s ok to own up to a mistake. We’re only human and no one is perfect. Ultimately that leads to greater accountability because there is an honesty at the heart of it. It removes the bullshit and gives folks the support they need to own their accomplishments, warts and all. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo

17. SET CLEAR EXPECTATIONS

Every employee plays a role in the company’s overall success, but depending on their level or access to senior leadership, they may not see how their contributions impact the greater whole. What is important to the CEO? What are the growth ambitions of the company? How does each individual’s responsibilities ladder up to the organization’s goals? It is essential to set clear expectations for each person, provide honest feedback, and communicate transparently about how daily activities and individual performance are linked to company success. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners

18. WRITE IT DOWN

Accountability holds when the measure is agreed before the work starts. Clarity is kindness, as they say. Set it together, write it down, and review it on a fixed schedule so a missed target shows up early and gets treated as information. People get defensive when the standard appears after the result, or when it shifts depending on who’s asking. Other than that, I try to give real guidelines and real feedback. If you start off that way, it instills the proper expectation of communication. — James Chester, WVN

19. DISCUSS HOW TO CLOSE THE PERFORMANCE-EXPECTATION GAP

I try to set a high bar of excellence by sharing great work, and by praising and rewarding excellent work. That way, when someone isn’t delivering, we can point to the gap between their performance and the expectation and talk about how to close the gap. It’s designed to create a supportive, safe, and fair environment. No finger pointing and passive-aggressiveness allowed! — Phillip Haid, Public Inc.

20. TAKE AN ASPIRATIONAL APPROACH

I’ve learned that empathy and accountability aren’t opposites. A few years ago, I leaned too far into being accommodating, and expectations slipped. I used to frame performance gaps as “We’re not where we need to be,” which I think created fear. Through coaching, I learned to take a more aspirational approach: “This is what excellence looks like. How can we get there?” It shifts the focus from fear to problem-solving. When people care deeply about the mission and understand what’s expected of them, accountability becomes a shared responsibility rather than something driven by fear. — Felicia Curcuru, Binti

21. REPLACE PUNITIVE REACTIONS WITH CURIOSITY AND COLLABORATION

Having experienced the damage of fear-based leadership early in my career, I know criticism and punishment only breed toxicity and burnout. Accountability without fear starts with connecting our work to purpose. At a mission-based organization, holding ourselves accountable is directly tied to achieving our mission. When performance issues arise, leaders should replace punitive reactions with curiosity and collaboration. Approaching staff with two-way dialogue to uncover blockers, rather than one-way scrutiny, turns accountability into a partnership that helps everyone succeed. — Jaymes Black, The Trevor Project

22. SEPARATE THE PERSON FROM THE OUTCOME

Accountability works best when expectations are clear before something goes wrong. I try to separate the person from the outcome, so the conversation becomes about what happened, what we learned, and what needs to change. Fear makes people hide problems. Clarity makes them easier to solve. — George Kailas, Prospero.ai

JEDEC puts next-gen DDR6 memory on a diet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a new design.

JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.

One of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.

JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.

Early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.

Baseline JEDEC Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s)

Peak Baseline Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s)

Notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.

Using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.

DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).

Consumer DDR5 memory modules currently sit at 64GB per module, while server RDIMMs have reached 512GB. DDR6 could raise module capacity to 128GB or 256GB and potentially scale RDIMMs to 1TB or more per slot.

DDR6 has no official launch date. Many believe 2029 is a realistic target for commercialization. However, in the current state of things, it would be a miracle if DDR6 had no setbacks.

#10629. Anthropic stock is already falling today: Why AI giants are seeing a painful sell-off after record IPO

Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.

And today things are even worse. Nearly every major hardware manufacturer that makes components for the AI pipeline—from CPUs to GPUs to memory—is seeing significant share price declines. 

And then there’s Anthropic itself, the world’s most valuable pure-play AI company. After a strong debut yesterday, its share price is down significantly this morning. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happening?

In premarket trading this morning, the tech-heavy Nasdaq is seeing red, along with some of the largest AI players that trade there.

As of this writing, Nasdaq futures are down nearly 1%. That’s after a significant fall of more than 550 points, or 2.25% yesterday. As of Thursday’s close, the Nasdaq was down around 5% for the week. 

Yesterday’s Nasdaq drop is all the more striking because it was also the day that Anthropic made its eagerly awaited market debut. The AI company’s IPO was priced at $83 per share, but those shares quickly popped to nearly $115 in early trading before ending the first day at $97.17—a 17% gain.

Anthropic’s IPO was the largest in history, raising around $81.3 billion. The company’s market cap now sits at around $1.27 billion, making it the 12th most valuable company on the planet.

Yet Anthropic’s success did little for the rest of the market. Throughout the day, tech stocks started falling, including those of other major AI players like Nvidia.

This morning, Asian markets and major AI and tech players are down significantly. And on this side of the Pacific, the sell-off is continuing with major American AI-related stocks.

As of the time of this writing, the following AI-adjacent stocks are down in premarket: 

  • Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMD): down 6.5%
  • NVIDIA Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA): down 2.3%
  • Intel Corporation (Nasdaq: INTC): down 5.2%
  • Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): down 4.8%
  • SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): down 6.7%

And yes, Anthropic’s stock price is down nearly 10%.

Why are Anthropic’s shares sinking?

Anthropic and hardware-related AI companies are both seeing their share prices sink in premarket trading, but maybe for different reasons.

When it comes to AI hardware companies, those that make the components needed to power the massive server farms AI data centers require, there has been significant negative sentiment around them since at least October.

Investors are increasingly getting uneasy with the major hyperscalers’ capex spending.

Companies like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions to build out data centers, and most aren’t yet showing a clear path to monetizing AI enough to recoup those costs.

If those companies cave to investor pressure and start scaling back their capex plans, it will hit AI hardware component makers (like Nvidia, Intel, and AMD) and memory makers (like Micron and SanDisk) pretty hard.

Investors seem to be bracing for an inevitable capex pullback, which has weighed heavily on hardware-adjacent AI stocks recently.

Other factors that have affected AI stocks lately include the Jensen Huang scandal and the ongoing fears that we are firmly in an AI bubble.

But Anthropic doesn’t make hardware, and it just had its successful IPO only yesterday—so why are its shares down so much today?

It likely has less to do with significant fears of capex spending and more to do with other factors.

The primary factor is likely profit-taking. The company’s stock price rose more than 17% on its first day of trading. Many shareholders who aren’t bound by lockup periods are likely taking some of those profits this morning.

Another factor—and one that could have significantly more long-term consequences—is that fears of an AI bubble and an AI slowdown are also likely weighing on investors’ minds. 

Anthropic has a massive valuation north of $1.2 trillion, but in the first nine months of 2026, the company generated only around $33 billion in revenue. Its net loss for the same period was $104 billion. Investors may be able to live with that discrepancy while the AI hype train is riding high, but enthusiasm only goes so far, and if the AI bubble bursts, Anthropic could be hit hard.

Where do Anthropic shares go from here?

That’s something everyone wants to know, and no one can tell you.

The company’s share price has already fallen from its intraday debut high of nearly $115 per share to its current premarket price of $88.44.

Contrast that with the company Anthropic just dethroned as having the largest IPO in history: SpaceX. 

When SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) went public in June, it was, until yesterday, the biggest IPO in history, raising $75 billion. Its IPO price was $135 per share, and the stock quickly jumped to more than $225 per share.

But then it began falling.

A month after its debut, SPCX shares were trading below their $135 IPO price as the hype wore off, and people began questioning the company’s future profitability. As of the time of this writing, SPCX shares are trading at just $131.66 in premarket trading.

If ANT’s early life plays out the same way—and there’s no way to predict whether it will or won’t—the share price could be underwater for even IPO investors in just a few months. And if the AI bubble does burst, things could get even worse.

#10626. Texas Democrats’ sweeping victory could spell trouble for Elon Musk’s business empire

Hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man said at The New York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections.

It’s easy to see why he feels that way, particularly in Texas, where Musk has moved his business operations and cultivated close ties with Republican leadership. Despite his extraordinary spending—$446 million, roughly half of which went to races in Texas—Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and swept the major statewide elections. That eye-popping figure includes $5 million for Republican incumbent Greg Abbott’s gubernatorial campaign and $10 million for Attorney General Ken Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid, both of which ended in defeat.

But Musk may soon have much bigger financial headaches than any futile campaign contributions. The incoming Democratic administration in Austin could complicate the billionaire’s plans to expand his sprawling business empire. Indeed, Texas’s governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has already signaled that she intends to be less accommodating of the kinds of tax breaks and land deals that helped lure Musk to the Lone Star State in the first place.

Abbott has by contrast been an enthusiastic champion of Musk’s Texas vision, appearing alongside him at company events and celebrating his investments in the state. Abbott and Musk reportedly keep in close contact, and the governor’s office even fought to prevent the release of months of communications with the tech mogul’s companies, arguing that they contain “information that is intimate and embarrassing and not of legitimate concern to the public.”

With Hinojosa in office, Musk can no longer count on that same level of intimacy, though he did offer a more sanguine assessment of his future in a blue Texas at the DealBook conference, predicting that Hinojosa would govern as a moderate. “I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said.

Billions in tax breaks

Musk’s companies have to date been given the royal treatment from the state. SpaceX, for instance, scored roughly $1.66 billion in potential property tax breaks for its planned Terafab semiconductor facility in Grimes County, between College Station and Houston, according to the Houston Chronicle. The incentives, approved by two local school districts under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program, could cut the company’s school property taxes in half for 10 years per phase of construction. SpaceX also secured a $30 million grant from the Texas Enterprise Fund.

Hinojosa has made no secret of her disdain for such arrangements. “I do think we should wipe clean corporate welfare in this state,” she told the Texas Standard in October, singling out Musk’s billion-dollar-plus tax break. She’s also pushing to reveal to the public more about Musk’s relationship with Abbott. In October, she sued Abbott for access to unredacted emails involving Musk and his companies.

But Hinojosa won’t have an easy time undoing those incentives. She would have considerable discretion over the Texas Enterprise Fund, although recovering money already awarded would depend on the grant’s terms. Reversing the much larger property tax breaks would prove far more difficult.

Those agreements are made among the company, local school districts, and the governor, who cannot simply terminate them over a change in policy. State law does allow the governor to revoke the incentives if a company fails to meet certain employment or wage requirements, but even then, the company must be given an opportunity to remedy or challenge the violation. To that end, Hinojosa has said she plans on reviewing Musk’s existing incentives to ensure his companies are meeting employment obligations. Those requirements can be remarkably lenient: Per the Chronicle, SpaceX needs to create just 80 jobs at its Terafab facility to meet the minimum employment threshold for the school-district tax incentives.

SpaceX’s South Texas expansion

Hinojosa’s victory could also throw a wrench into SpaceX’s expansion plans in South Texas, where the company is pursuing massive new infrastructure projects—and seeking additional land for its operations.

For starters, there’s the $24 billion data center and natural gas-fired power plant planned near its Starbase headquarters near the border with Mexico. SpaceX announced the project earlier this month and says construction activity has already created more than 3,000 jobs, though the facility is not yet operational. (That project has already encountered resistance from local officials, with Cameron County commissioners voting this week 3–2 against advancing SpaceX’s request for a 10-year, 100% property-tax abatement for the project.)

Hinojosa has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center approvals until Texas lawmakers enact stronger protections for water supplies, electricity customers, and surrounding communities. And she’s also indicated that projects already underway wouldn’t necessarily be exempt: “If it needs a permit that the state has to approve, then that’s on hold,” she told the Chronicle last week.

Again, though, SpaceX has gotten a head start. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality this week approved an air permit for a natural gas plant associated with the project. But that permit covers only the power-generating component, not the entire $24 billion development. So Hinojosa could still hold up the project if SpaceX needs additional state approvals once she takes office.

Meanwhile, SpaceX has also been pursuing a deal to acquire state-owned parkland near its Boca Chica launch facility, at the mouth of the Rio Grande. Texas Monthly reported last month that state officials were considering selling 1,300 acres to the company, raising obvious questions around coastal access and habitat preservation. Hinojosa, who grew up in nearby Brownsville, asked the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department shortly after her election to hold off on any action during the transition. SpaceX has since clarified that it wants approximately 1,200 acres of public parkland surrounding its launch facility—not Boca Chica Beach itself—and says it would preserve half the property as coastal habitat.

And SpaceX could face another headache at Boca Chica. Benjamin Flores, the Democrat who is the incoming Texas land commissioner, plans to challenge a 2013 law allowing temporary beach closures for rocket launches, Texas Monthly reports. And while the state Supreme Court threw out a previous challenge in June, that rejection came on procedural grounds, leaving the law’s constitutionality unresolved.

A possible Tesla–SpaceX merger

Tesla and SpaceX have been discussing a merger, which would bring Musk’s EV, rocket, satellite and AI businesses under one corporate roof. The state’s new Democratic leadership could throw a wrench into those plans. 

Texas’s incoming attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has already signaled that he intends to take a very close look at any such tie-up. “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny,” he told Bloomberg last week, citing concerns about corporate concentration.

Johnson’s office could investigate potential antitrust violations and, if deemed warranted, challenge the merger in court. Unlike Hinojosa’s proposed data center restrictions, which could require new legislation or regulations, that authority already exists under state law.|

#10624. WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

“WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta update, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

#10623. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

The agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

We wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

Which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

The formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

Relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

On 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure."

Before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

The measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:

This time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

One detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a new colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

An agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and said it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

The --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

An agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer new to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

These are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

Take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've just had a few high-stakes security vulnerabilities making systems administrators run around with their heads on fire, and the deluge doesn't look like it's stopping any time soon. Java, the programming language that Oracle has always claimed is on billions of devices, has a critical security vulnerability that allows for remote code execution (RCE), often without even needing to log in to the application. The consequence is that an attacker can gain access to the target system, read user and internal data, and have a launch point for further shenanigans, including database access and potential system takeover.

The flaw was dubbed Java4Shell by Calif Research, the lab that found the vulnerability. The researchers say it rates 9.2 on the newer CVSS 4.0 scale, though individual reports from companies like Oracle itself and Red Hat give it their own ratings, but they're all in the 8 to 9.8 range depending on the vendor. The root cause is a bug in OpenJDK, the library that nearly every distribution of Java, whether Oracle's or anyone else's, derives their implementations from.

You can see an exploit of the bug in action below across multiple software services.

The actual bug is a flaw in an optimization for Base64 decoding, functionality that's ubiquitous in any programming language. Base64 is a format to allow for easy transformation of binary data into plain text. In the modern day, it's used to embed files in the middle of text, like inserting image data in the middle of HTML or CSS, attaching files to emails (internally they're all text-based), or simply representing data as text for visual inspection, like file checksums or cryptographic key fingerprints.

Oracle has already fixed the bug and issued updated versions of its wares. However, much like digital certificates, operating systems and even individual programs include their own copy of a Java executable, meaning that the potential blast radius is far wider than you'd expect at first glance. Calif listed many such common applications: at the time of the post, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and PingFederate all had full unauthenticated RCE, while Apache Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker have RCEs after authentication.

Because Java is so darn widespread, most every company has to issue security advisories and updates for their wares, including IBM, Red Hat, Siemens, and Broadcom. Because so many containers also use Java-based applications in some form, those too are vulnerable, and the count of individual vulnerable container images across registries everywhere is likely a high figure. This is likely not a bug that will be easily eradicated.

There is a condition to trigger the exploit, but it's not too difficult to fulfill. The Java instance in question must be running on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 support and the VBMI extension. In practice, that means chips from the Intel Ice Lake and AMD Zen 4 families, from 2021 and 2022 respectively, for their server variants. Older CPUs are not affected, as the code optimization that contains the bug is specific to VBMI.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The specific bug is in a hand-written assembly optimization that fails a simple bounds check. If an attacker inputs 64 As and an "=" sign as padding, they can overwrite neighboring memory, and then weaponize that corruption, similar to how Heartbleed worked. As usual these days, Calif says that the vulnerability was found by an AI bot, with $200 worth of tokens. Though unlike many other examples, this one was actually fairly deep, and it wasn't low-hanging fruit that illustrated poor code or network security hygiene.

#10621. Peeping AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy,’ says Meredith Whittaker, so Signal is blocking screenshots

AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions. 

Signal is the latest platform to make changes. The encrypted messaging app is preventing screenshots on any device with Apple’s iOS 27 in a bid to stop AI agents from accessing sensitive information. It will also block AI assistants from capturing screen data on Android devices. 

“An existential threat’

Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal Technology Foundation, the nonprofit that runs the Signal app, announced the change in a blog post.

Whittaker pointed to how Google, Apple, and Microsoft’s “agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”

The app can now block Siri AI and turn on “screen security” as a means of preventing AI assistants from scanning information. Users can turn off the protections, but Signal warns that this could leave messages exposed and remove the app’s privacy guarantee. 

Signal took similar measures last year on Windows 11 to protect messages from Microsoft Recall, a feature that periodically captures and stores screenshots of your work.

Signal is fed up with a lack of AI assistant transparency

The current blog post seeps with frustration at Signal’s inability to do more to protect privacy amid a lack of transparency from tech giants.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal—and application developers beyond—lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” says Whittaker. 

She explained that Signal has struggled due to limited information about how any of these AI agents work, being forced to do its own forensic investigations into how the “AI systems access application data.” 

The blog post calls on makers of major operating systems to provide tools and information about how the AI agents work and how they can be prevented from accessing sensitive data.

She further said that apps should have a way to opt out of AI tools like screen reading without having to compromise their core utility. 

Whittaker issues a clear warning: “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.”

#10618. How Thanksgiving travelers are feeling about holiday air travel after widespread tech outages

At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026’s busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there’s another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She’s pretty sure she’s not the only one.

“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having … I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.

It’s an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days’ tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it’s a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it’s one they’re likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.

But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”

Air travel is vital — and taken for granted

In some ways, the country’s aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy … and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

“You’ve got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There’s nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”

At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she’s used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she’s not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she’s not rattled by it.

“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.

She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”

And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to “Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something,” she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”

The expense can be as much of an obstacle as the delays

If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can’t just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.

Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.

Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.

It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter’s flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.

She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.

The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She’s keeping the rolls in her garage

“The funny part,” she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”

AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

—Deepti Hajela, Associated Press
