#10615. ‘Worst COP ever’? Climate talks in Turkey are near the finish line and activists are in an uproar

This year’s U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators fighting over how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.

Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.

Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding.

Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, said they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday.

Worries about a ‘worst COP ever’

Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year’s disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding.

If fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa.

In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed.

“The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.”

In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

“There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!”

As climate talks near their end, fossil fuel debate rages

One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.

But the final draft doesn’t spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push.

“At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa.

The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change.

Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time.

Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31, are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text’s draft.

“We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey’s Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said.

“Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere,” said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.”

Vulnerable nations say climate finance is lacking

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don’t emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change.

They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need.

The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft’s previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually.

Many of the world’s most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year’s talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter.

It’s richer nations, like the U.S., that vulnerable countries want funding from — and it’s hard to ask for funds without American officials in the room.

Efforts to slow global warming have essentially stalled for the past five years, according to a recent report by the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker.

“Disappointment is rife,” said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, an adviser to African negotiators in Turkey. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

“Hope is not lost, but absent a course correction, we are headed toward a low-ambition set of outcomes at COP31,” he said.

Associated Press writer Tammy Webber contributed to this report.

—Suzan Fraser, Anton L. Delgado, Sibi Arasu and Victoria Milko Associated Press

#10611. Parents are prioritizing screen-free gifts this season as research about potential harms to children piles up

As everyday technology becomes more advanced, parents are prioritizing screen-free, hands-on holiday gifts for children. 

Forty-one percent of people buying gifts for kids in their family are leaning toward screen-free gifts, according to a survey by PwC. 

A Germany-based brand called Tonies created an interactive, screen-free audio player designed for children.

The most well-known toy, called the Toniebox, is a squishy, cube-shaped speaker controlled completely by the child. Models come with a hand-painted, magnetic figurine that automatically plays audiobooks, songs, or stories when placed on the box. 

Last holiday season, the Tonies app hit No. 1 on the App Store. This year, the company saw a 33% increase in global revenue in the first nine months of 2026. Its biggest market is North America, capturing $315 million in revenue in 2025. 

Concerns about screen use in childhood

Screen use in early years of childhood has shown potential to harm cognitive, linguistic, and social-emotional growth, according to a study from the National Library of Medicine.

Excessive screen use among youth has even been linked to a rise in likelihood of obesity, sleep disorders, and depression, and anxiety, the study found.

Screens have the potential to improve education and learning, when paired with parental controls and screen-time restrictions. But, Tonies offers a chance for children to interact with their minds rather than a touch-screen. 

“Through listening, the key thing is, your imagination develops because you actually picture the dragon, you picture the knight, you picture whatever it is. It’s not just delivered for you,” Mark McColgan, general manager, North America at Tonies, told Fast Company. 

The company started producing the Toniebox 10 years ago, and while new versions are released, the boxes are built for long-term use, said McColgan, who joined Tonies this year from Mattel.

The boxes are a relief for busy parents, too. Sometimes parents need a moment to themselves, but offering a screen to their children for a short-term distraction can become a long-term addiction, and a source of guilt for parents.

Some parents have turned to screens to curb behavior in public, and sometimes, as a replacement for expensive childcare, a study from a hospital found.

“It gives them guilt-free time to do something else, because when their child is playing with the Toniebox, they know it’s a safe, good environment for them to do so,” McColgan said. 

This story was updated to clarify that new versions of the Toniebox have been released since the product launched.

#10609. The internet’s doomsday preppers are having a field day with all the tech outages

What do you keep in your emergency bag? The one for when the electrical grid goes down. Or all the banks stop working. Or the world is ending.

First aid essentials. N95 masks. A pocket-size book of human anatomy. Solar-powered chargers and small knives. A compass and a road atlas of the continental U.S. That’s what Gina Arconti keeps in her Béis Weekender bag in case of emergencies. “Something some people don’t know about me is I’m a little bit of a doomsday prepper,” she said in a recent TikTok video, now with over 400,000 views.

The video was posted last week, after Microsoft Outlook went down. Then flights across the U.S. were grounded. Then Apple Pay stopped working. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network temporarily went down. You don’t have to be a conspiracy theorist to wonder what’s going on.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

But for longtime doomsday preppers, the writing is on the wall.

“Amazon doomsday haul,” Jeff For, another TikTok user based in Los Angeles, said in a video posted earlier this month. His purchases include a hand-crank portable radio that doubles as a flashlight, phone charger, compass, and SOS signal. He also bought a collapsible water jug, candles, and a mini drone. “If I’m stuck or I don’t want to leave where I am I can use this bad boy to fly up in the air and see everything around me,” he explains.

Some are rushing to stock up on supplies from Costco or $395 emergency backpacks containing everything from a pop-up tube tent to dried ice cream. Others have been squirreling away supplies for years, preparing for this exact moment.

Online preppers are also seeing a surge of views amid the outages. “So you just started your prepping journey and you’re not really sure what the next step will be,” said Krystal, known online as the “Doomsday Queen,” to her 132,000 Instagram followers earlier this month. The video’s caption directs viewers to her free Beginner’s Preparedness Guide.

Others preach off-grid self-sufficiency, offering tutorials on food storage, emergency water supplies, and what to do when the toilets no longer flush.

But some may be overlooking the first rule of doomsday prep: Don’t tell anyone about your doomsday prep. Otherwise, where do you think everyone will head when the world actually ends?

#10607. What is Model Routing in AI?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

"Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below shows a typical AI model routing architecture.

Model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan users go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

The big platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google says Gemini Notebook uses its new Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

We'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

The test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

Put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:

Confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

The second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:

If Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

Model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:

Speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

The choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

The loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:

The return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

Several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:

Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

The ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

OpenRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

OpenClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

#10605. The Nvidia CEO scandal is impacting Asian American women in tech and academia. Here’s how

The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent. But what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy.

Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media.

“So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women,” said Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people’s opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.”

Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal will diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It’s a reminder that no accomplishments will completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes.

Jensen Huang has since resigned. However, the U.S. Justice Department has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy.

“I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” President Donald Trump told reporters this week.

Asian women struggle to be taken seriously as leaders

Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.”

Depicting them like trophy wives “implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University.

The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions.

“I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. It’s not funny to her or me.”

Many clients of Stand with Asian Americans are Asian women who have proved their competence yet are still accused of being fraudulent or deceitful, said Rachel Lee, the organization’s president and general counsel.

“It is deeply disturbing to see this not just unique to the Nvidia Jensen Huang case, but as a part of a long-standing dangerous narrative that Asians are perpetual foreigners, untrustworthy, disloyal,” Lee said.

On top of their integrity being questioned, Asian workers also deal with misconceptions that they cannot lead. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the United States Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of U.S. adults characterized Asian Americans in the workplace as “respectful” or “reliable.” Only 1 in 10 viewed them as “assertive.”

“The No. 1 theme in onboarding interviews all last week were ‘I’m mistaken for the secretary, I don’t look like the typical face of leadership,” said Chien, talking about new members of her Asian leaders network.

Stereotypes around Asian women go back centuries

Years before Chinese laborers were fully banned from entering the U.S. under the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the federal government targeted immigrant Asian women. In 1875, Congress passed the Page Act to control immigration from “any Oriental country.” It included a specific prohibition of women coming for prostitution.

“Chinese women were deemed — and East Asian women in general — as being untrustworthy,” Chai said. “It was presumed that they would be coming for illicit means as prostitutes to the United States and that would cause harm to white men.”

By the early 20th century, the Asian woman as a seductress, spy or “dragon lady” started becoming an archetype on Hollywood screens, she added.

The headlines had Chien reflecting on when she played a spy in a building security ad in Hong Kong 20 years ago. She was instructed to wear three bras to resemble Angelina Jolie’s figure. She wrote an Instagram post to point out “how the media enjoys putting Asian women in that kind of role” and urged women to not let people’s assumptions keep them from success.

“So many followers messaged me saying ‘thank you so much for speaking up,'” Chien said.

Real harm can come from stereotypes

Suspicion toward Chinese people in the U.S. has dramatically heightened geopolitical tensions. Over two dozen states in the last few years have proposed or enacted “alien land laws” to prevent Chinese nationals from buying property. The number of international students enrolling in American universities has fallen. And the first Trump administration created a plan known as the ” China Initiative ” to crack down on espionage by profiling Chinese professors.

Critics say that initiative contributed to the 2024 suicide of Jane Ying Wu. A neuroscientist at Northwestern University who had lived in the U.S. for 40 years, the 60-year-old came under federal investigation in 2019. She was never charged with anything.

“This type of pernicious stereotype can actually destroy lives,” Chai said. “It’s not in any way an accurate portrait of an entire race and ethnicity.”

Jokes rooted in stereotypes under the guise of being complimentary also do not help Asian female workers, Lee added.

“Whether it’s a compliment or not, a trope is a trope,” she said. “I don’t care if it comes out of the mouth of the U.S. president.”

Ideally, Lee said more companies should allow for education and training around the harm and history of stereotypes. She encourages any woman who has had uncomfortable interactions to reach out to advocacy groups such as Stand with Asian Americans if she has nobody to turn to at work. At Stand with Asian Americans, people do not need to have a legal case of discrimination or harassment to receive assistance including education on their rights and mental health support.

Individuals also have the right to draw boundaries and make clear what’s not OK to say, Lee added. It’s in employers’ best interest to make sure no federal laws against discrimination and harassment are being violated.

“It’s a win-win to have that conversation,” Lee said.

—Terry Tang, Associated Press

#10604. YouTube ‘Co-Views’ try to guess how many people are watching your TV, rolling out now

Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube says it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

In a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

YouTube says it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”

How is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”

#10601. Gold is falling to lows not seen in more than a year: 3 reasons why the precious metal is getting crushed

It’s not just tech and AI stocks getting hammered lately.

Gold investors are also seeing significant losses. As of this writing, the precious metal is down nearly 3% for the day, trading just above $3,576 per ounce. That’s a level the yellow bullion has not seen since September 2025.

That price is all the more striking when contrasted with gold’s surging value earlier this year. In January, gold peaked at around $5,600. But since then, the precious metal has been under constant pressure, and in late September, its price began plummeting from around $4,400 an ounce to roughly $800 less today.

But just what is driving gold’s fall as of late? There seem to be three major factors impacting the bullion’s recent plunge.

Expected Fed interest rate hikes

The first factor likely influencing gold’s fall recently is the likelihood of a federal interest rate hike in December. As Fast Company previously reported, the Fed is likely to raise rates by 25 basis points, to a range of 4.00%–4.25%.

When interest rates rise, money becomes more expensive to borrow. This means the lenders of that money stand to make more. Anyone can become a “lender” by buying Treasury bills whose interest rates are heavily tied to the Fed’s set rates.

Rising interest rates typically lead investors to sell off non-interest-yielding assets and use the proceeds to buy assets—like Treasury bills—that return a guaranteed rate.

This asset reallocation is likely one of the major factors affecting gold prices (and not just gold—but also cryptocurrency prices lately).

The tech and AI sell-off

The second likely major factor impacting gold prices lately actually has nothing to do with gold itself. Rather, the rut in tech and AI stocks can be to blame.

Since October, tech and AI stocks have been under sustained pressure as investors have grown increasingly concerned about what many see as out-of-control, unsustainable capital expenditure by AI hyperscalers.

Critics argue that this massive capex spending—to the tune of hundreds of billions—can’t last unless the hyperscalers can start generating sizable returns, something they have so far been unable to do.

Investors worry that if revenue (and profits) can’t materialize, the hyperscalers will cut back capex, sending the business of AI component makers like Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Micron, and more into a downward spiral.

As these concerns take hold, investors are moving out of high-volatility tech and AI stocks, taking profits and sending shares lower. But not everyone is taking profits. Some investors are cutting their losses, and when they do, they also tend to sell other liquid assets, like gold, to cover them.

A stronger U.S. dollar

Finally, another problem for gold is the increasing strength of the U.S. dollar. Since September, the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) has increased by more than 4%.

The DXY tracks the U.S. dollar’s value relative to six foreign currencies: the Euro, Yen, Pound, Swedish Krona, Swiss Franc, and Canadian Dollar.

A strengthening dollar can be a problem for gold because the bullion is priced in U.S. dollars.

When U.S. dollars become more valuable relative to foreign currencies, international demand for gold usually slips because it costs foreign investors more to buy the precious metal.

#10599. When the client is a good fit on paper, but still not a good fit

I was so excited to work with a new client. 

A perfect match for my expertise, and the type of company I prefer collaborating with. Meeting the client for an exploratory call felt like a dream. A well-respected brand to add to my portfolio.

But once the contract was signed, it was a struggle from day one. We parted ways six months later. 

Most advice about struggling client relationships assumes there is an obvious problem, like that the client is overly demanding or hard to reach. But in this case, it was something else. The vibes were off. When that happens, it’s less obvious what to fix. 

Recognizing the difference between a difficult client and a poor fit can help you decide sooner whether to adjust the working relationship or simply walk away.


Why a client can look right on paper and still not work

The things I vet for during the sales process can be different from the things that make a working relationship successful. 

Before signing, I look at the potential client’s industry and the scope of work. The client’s budget has to be aligned with my rate, and I have to feel confident that I can deliver what the client is asking for. That’s the relationship “on paper.”

But what’s often unknown is how the client interacts with a consultant or contractor (like me). I’m also unaware of any internal politics at the company that might impact the working relationship. Those details usually become apparent once I start delivering actual work. 

Is it a difficult client or a poor fit?

A difficult client has problems like not paying on time or asking for work outside of the scope. These can be fixed (or at least managed) with a solid contract and clear boundaries. Most of the biggest client red flags that solopreneurs face are in this category.

A poor fit is different. The client may pay on time and stay within scope, but other parts of the working relationship feel strained. Maybe stakeholder feedback gets under your skin because of how it’s presented. Or you find yourself dreading the work, even though, on paper, it’s what you had agreed to do.

One thing to ask yourself: Would a different consultant or contractor have the same trouble with this client? If the answer is yes, you’re likely dealing with a difficult client. But if you can picture someone else doing great work for them, the problem is probably the fit.

A second question: If this client always pays on time and never asks for anything outside of scope, would you still want the work? A “no” usually means that fit is the issue.

What to try before you walk away

A poor fit sometimes might improve if you’re able to directly address the thing that’s causing you angst. It’s worth trying before you decide.

If the problem is, for example, “too many cooks” providing you with feedback and contradictory opinions, you might be able to solve this. Something like:

“It’s easier for me to make sure I deliver what you need if you consolidate your feedback. Can you work on your end to send me a list of thoughts/changes? That way, I don’t start down one path only to find that you want me to go in a different direction.”

In some cases, your client might be willing to change—they may simply not have experience working with a contractor or consultant. 

You might also give yourself a checkpoint, like an additional month of work after the conversation. If nothing has changed by then, you have your answer.

Admitting the relationship isn’t working

When you work solo, a poor fit can drag you down. In a company, a colleague might take over the account, or a manager could reassign the work. As a solopreneur, there’s no one to hand it to. And since your income depends on the work, ending the relationship means replacing that revenue.

But staying has a cost. Stress. Frustration. All the things you were supposed to escape by choosing a solopreneur life instead of a corporate job.

If the conversation with your client doesn’t change anything, more effort probably won’t fix it. At that point, calling it a poor fit and moving on is a business decision. 

It helps to remember that a poor fit says nothing about your skills or the client’s character. It simply didn’t work out.
